newsitem.title: USA: Panic across U.S. over immigration law changes.
newsitem.headline: Panic across U.S. over immigration law changes.

text.p: With only a few days left before the imposition of sweeping changes in laws affecting immigrants, foreigners across the United States have been sent into a panic of uncertainty, fear and anger.

In Miami, where about half of all residents were born outside the United States, hundreds of people line up daily, many before dawn, to ask Immigration & Naturalisation Service (INS) officers about how the legal changes will affect their status and those of their loved ones.
Similar lines have been reported elsewhere in the country.
INS officials say the changes that will be effective from Tuesday as a result of the Republican-backed Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 are not that significant.

But immigrants and their legal advocates scoff at INS claims that there is no reason for panic, saying the situation is even more serious because of pending changes in welfare laws that deny government benefits even to legal immigrants.

The new rules make deportation easier and faster, make it harder for new illegal immigrants to establish themselves in the United States and toughen penalties for illegals who are caught in this country.

"When I saw the line, I wanted to cry," said Sandra Clare, a Brazilian citizen who married her husband Andrew, a U.S. citizen from Deerfield Beach, Florida, on Feb. 8 and rushed to change her status on Tuesday as soon as the mail arrived with their paperwork in fear of missing the April 1 deadline.
"We just want to get it in today," she said, shaking her head as she waited behind several hundred people who had not even made it into the INS lobby.

In San Diego and Los Angeles, immigrants who have lived in California for years have been trying to get border police to arrest them before April 1, gambling that if they are caught after that date they stand little chance of winning the right to remain in this country.

Across the country, lines for marriage licenses in cities with many immigrants stretch for hours as newcomers hope to benefit from tying the knot with legal residents and citizens. "In my 11 years here this is the biggest increase in marriages I've ever seen," New York Clerk Carlos Cuevas said.

After April 1, illegal immigrants caught after six months in the country will be banned from returning for three years. Those who stay illegally for a year or more face a 10-year ban. And the law makes it far more difficult to win "suspension of deportation," a reprieve given to long-term illegal residents considered to be of good moral character.

The law also establishes a one-year time frame for residents to request political asylum, affecting those with temporary visas as well as illegal immigrants. Those who arrive at borders, airports and ports requesting asylum must be prepared immediately to show a risk of persecution at home or face deportation without a hearing.

"Thousands of people who have lived in the United States for years will no longer be able to apply for permanent residence," Cheryl Little, an attorney at the Florida Immigrant Advocacy Centre, said. "In Miami alone this will affect thousands of Nicaraguans, Salvadoreans, Guatemalans, Cubans, Haitians and others who have worked hard, paid taxes, and played by the rules."
Everyone agrees the situation has not been helped by what has been termed a virtual industry of misinformation.

The INS said filing paperwork or getting married before April 1 provided no advantage but immigrants, many of whom tried and failed to get information from the INS over the phone, said they had heard differently.

Gamaliel Fanfan, 43, a legal resident from Haiti whose wife is a U.S. citizen, said he was taking no chances as he waited in the Miami INS line to apply for entry permits for the two children he left in Haiti nine years ago.

"I listened to the radio and they said that if the people don't get their green cards here by April 1, they will send them back to the country where they came from," he said. "I just want to get my children here."
